title: わざと — “on purpose / deliberately”
summary: An adverb meaning that someone does something deliberately, knowing what the result will be. It goes right before a verb and often implies the person had a reason such as teasing or revenge. The opposite idea is うっかり (by mistake).

patterns.form: わざと＋動詞（普通形・過去形など）
わざと＋動詞ない形＋ない／ようだ
patterns.gloss: deliberately not do ～ / seems on purpose

body.p: わざと tells the listener that the action was not an accident. 彼はわざと負けた: he lost knowingly, for instance to let someone else win. It is placed before the verb it modifies.
The sentence often has a reason with ために or ようと: 笑わせようと、わざと変な顔をした. The action itself can be kind, playful or unkind, so context shows the attitude.

body.h: Compare with わざわざ and 故意に
body.p: わざわざ is “take the trouble to” and is about effort, not hidden intention. 故意に is the stiff, written version of わざと, often used for bad actions (故意に壊した). Use わざと in everyday speech.

examples.ja: 彼（かれ）はわざと負（ま）けたようだ。
examples.romaji: Kare wa wazato maketa you da.
examples.tr: It seems he lost on purpose.

examples.ja: 弟（おとうと）を笑（わら）わせようと、わざと変（へん）な顔（かお）をした。
examples.romaji: Otouto o warawaseyou to, wazato hen na kao o shita.
examples.tr: I made a funny face on purpose to make my little brother laugh.

examples.ja: 相手（あいて）を怒（おこ）らせるために、わざとひどいことを言（い）った。
examples.romaji: Aite o okoraseru tame ni, wazato hidoi koto o itta.
examples.tr: He said something cruel on purpose to make the other person angry.

pitfalls: Do not confuse わざと (hidden intention) with わざわざ (taking the trouble). They look alike but differ in meaning.
わざと is not used for a plan the speaker proudly announces; it sounds like admitting to something.
